doc.title: Ashley Keating and Allan Whitworth Interview, 1963-03-22

chapter: Early life and the Brisbane band
title: Growing up in Queensland, discovering New Orleans style, learning banjo
summary: Keating was born in Queensland in 1939; his father was a cornet champion. Records by Muggsy Spanier led him to New Orleans style. He took up banjo about two and a half years earlier and had ten lessons.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: In Wandi, a small town in Queensland, Australia, Dick. And when? 1939, December the 1st. December the 1st.
And did you hear jazz when you were growing up? Did you have any musicians in your family or anything?

My father, at one stage, won the Queensland Band Cornet Solo Championship. He was a relatively good musician, I'd say. I, at some stage of the game, when very small, can remember listening to Dixieland and having it appeal to me, not really knowing quite what it was. It was a pseudo type, I'd say. And soon, via Muggsy Spanier and bands of that ilk, the Bobcats, found out that I could get the sound the whole way through a record, not just parts of it. And that started my interest in the New Orleans style.
You came back through the Chicago and the Dixieland, I hope, people, to the New Orleans.
And, uh, did you play any instrument before you took up the banjo?

No, it was the first instrument. A last desperate effort, I'd say. I don't think I could have mastered anything else. Not that I've mastered this, but it was the one that could get me onto the scene quicker than any other, I'd say.
Uh-huh. And, uh, when did you start the banjo?
Uh, it'll be two and a half years ago now.
Two and a half years ago? Uh-huh. And did you have any lessons to start with?
Uh, yes, I had ten lessons from a, a woman teacher at the Queensland College of Music. Hmm.
They teach banjo at the Queensland College of Music?
Yes, they do. It's a commercial type of, uh, uh, solely teaches popular music. She taught me where to find the notes and a few chord formations. From there I pressed on on her own.
Did she have a clue about what you were trying to do?

Uh, she half understood, I think. She, she knew I wanted to play chords and wasn't particularly interested in becoming a virtuoso. But, uh, I don't think she knew who Lawrence Mariro was. And who is Lawrence Mariro to you? Uh, well, he still is everything I want to be as far as a musician goes. Uh, I can't recall ever hearing a more thrilling, uh, sound on the banjo.
